The mention of "posterior mediastinum" in B might be a distractor or specific pathology detail, but the spatial relationship (Right Mass -> Left Deviation) is physically correct in B, whereas A claims "rightward deviation" which is visually false.

Let's re-read carefully.
Image 1: Mass is on the patient's RIGHT (viewer's left). Trachea (star) is pushed to the patient's LEFT (viewer's right).
Option A: "causing ... rightward deviation". False.
Option B: "causes leftward deviation ... occupies right hemithorax". True spatial relationship. "exerting pressure from the posterior mediastinum". The lateral view (Fig 2) shows the mass (white arrows) extending along the spine/posteriorly? Actually, the white arrows in Fig 2 point to the posterior chest wall/spine area, but the star is anterior/mid. Wait, looking at Fig 2, the black arrows point to the trachea which is displaced posteriorly? No, the star is the trachea. The white arrows in Fig 2 point to the posterior ribs/vertebrae? Or is it a posterior mass?
Actually, let's look at the standard presentation of this case. This looks like a classic "Right sided mass pushing trachea left".
Option B says "leftward deviation". This matches the image.
Option A says "rightward deviation". This contradicts the image.
Therefore, B is the best answer regarding the direction of deviation relative to the mass location.

Answer: B
